newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - Romania pig, poultry farms face crisis.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Romania pig, poultry farms face crisis.

text.p: Marin Dumitrescu, head of the Suintest state pig farm shakes his head as seven years of post-communist innovation collide with the reformist government's drive to make agriculture pay its own way.

His staff start the working day in Fierbinti, 30 km (18 miles) northeast of Bucharest, wondering whether the farm, with its 20,000 pigs, will balance the books or face shutdown like other pig and poultry operations saddled with huge debts.

Dumitrescu says a government order for such farms to go private or enter into liquidation takes no account of the economics facing the sector -- high interest rates, low producer prices and evaporating foreign and domestic markets.
The government, he says, is hurtling forward with reforms of the state system with no clear idea what is to replace it.

"Many farms are simply no longer able to buy feed to keep their pigs going," Dumitrescu said in his simple, tidy office, dominated by the tricolor flag of Romania's 1989 revolution, the communist crest torn from the middle.
"Some farms have debts two or three times their assets. What investor wants to buy a farm like that? If we don't get some help next year, I don't know if we'll still be here."
LIVESTOCK A NATIONAL AFFAIR
Pigs and chickens have become affairs of state.
National television has shown bony piglets gnawing at iron pens or attacking each other as state farms crippled by debts grapple with an abrupt cut-off of state subsidies.
The latest joke among Romanians earning average monthly salaries equivalent to less than $100 is to describe a friend as being "as thin as a pig".
Statistics show that mortality rates of piglets have nearly doubled from normal Romanian rates of 15 to 20 percent. Farms succumbing to bankruptcy have lost up to 80 percent.

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea, who heads the centrist government after last year's elections, says the "profitable or bust" order was necessary to clear up the chaos left over by the half-hearted reforms of their ex-communist predecessors.
The government's immediate answer was to make available 100,000 tonnes of feed from state reserves.
"These farms have been badly managed, with emphasis on expanding the number of pigs, no matter the costs," Agriculture Minister Dinu Gavrilescu told reporters last month.
Dumitrescu rejects such arguments. He suggests his farm has done everything and more to adjust to new reality in the state sector, which raises 3.5 million of Romania's eight million pigs.

Suintest developed its own feed-producing plant and special drying silos to beat high grain prices, expanded storage areas to avoid paying extortionate rents and upgraded its abattoir -- all in the name of self-sufficiency.
FARM ECONOMICS DO NOT ADD UP

But a kilogram (2.2 lb) of pork costs 8,000 lei ($1.18) to produce and only fetches 5,200 lei on markets undergoing liberalisation, while costing a Bucharest supermarket shopper around 20,000. An attempt with other farms to set up retail shops -- and cut out expensive middlemen -- remains on paper.
The farm is one of only five in Romania producing top breeding stock.

But prices for those animals have plunged with cheap stock from nine failed farms flooding the market. Farms struggling to remain afloat spend little time or money, he says, on upholding genetic standards.
Market prices have been further depressed by a decline in annual per capita pork consumption by budget-conscious Romanians to 32 kg (70lb) last year from 53 kg (115 lb) in 1989.

Romanian pork does not meet European Union standards. Huge pre-1989 exports to the Soviet Union, in exchange for oil and gas, have dried up as suppliers have found Russian customs and trade rules "impenetrable".
Making his way through communist-era barns refurbished to save money on heating bills, Dumitrescu sighed as he pointed to an underdeveloped sow unsuitable for breeding.
"That's because we couldn't afford to buy some of the supplements and additives. We had to cut corners somewhere. This is where it has brought us," Dumitrescu said.

"It took two decades to acclimatise this Dutch breed to Romanian conditions," he said, pointing out a group of white Landrace in the next barn. "If we go under it will take another 20 years, starting from scratch."

Farming, he said, has been reduced to chaos by haste in dismantling the hated collective system instituted by pro-Moscow communists at the close of World War Two. The state sector now accounts for no more than 15 percent of the total.
"When they disbanded collective farms in 1990, people grabbed a door handle here, a window there and ended up with tiny plot and nothing to work it with," he said.
"I am for privatisation and more efficiency. But what sort of agriculture can you have now without technology? We find ourselves back at square one, the way we were in 1948."
UNMECHANISED LIFESTYLE IN THE VILLAGE
The bustling farm belies the unmechanised existence of Fierbinti village, even in the relative prosperity of the Bucharest region.
Bicycles and horse-drawn carts are the main mode of transport on rutted dirt roads. A top-heavy hay rack is hauled through the village centre by two men.
Suintest's 200 employees, who earn on average the equivalent of $60 per month before bonuses, have no illusions about their future.
The farm's chief economist catches up with Dumitrescu between barns to confer on a dossier. He confides that he found her crying one morning while contemplating the accounts.
Others wait for elusive foreign investors to save the day.

"Perhaps you can help us. Perhaps you know an investor who can help?" said Suinvest's veterinary surgeon Gheorghe Stan. "No. In the end I suppose God is the only one who can help." ($ = 6750 Romanian Lei)
